title: Overview and what is live
html:
Overview

Silicon is an original five-stage in-order RV32I processor (rtl/silicon_core.sv, 574 lines of SystemVerilog, Apache-2.0), verified against the official riscv-arch-test suite under Verilator, synthesized with Yosys to a generic gate library, and driven in this app by a browser twin that is trace-identical to the RTL.

What is live in the browser, and what is not

Part Where it runs Receipt
Pipeline simulation In the browser: core.js, a cycle-accurate model of the same microarchitecture Per-cycle trace identical to the Verilator and Icarus Verilog (iverilog) RTL runs on all 38 arch tests and all 19 programs (test/results/)
Gate-level activity In the browser: gatesim.js evaluates the real Yosys netlist (8,297 cells) every cycle Its port outputs are checked against the behavioural model every cycle; identical on all 38 arch tests (archtest-jsgate-vs-rtl.txt). The same netlist simulated with Verilator and Icarus Verilog matches the RTL on all 57 binaries (verilator-gate.md)
Assembly Live. Edit any program in the Assembly tab; it is assembled in the browser by Silicon's own two-pass assembler (asm.js) and loaded into memory Byte-identical to GNU as/ld on all curated programs (41 checks) and 110 random programs; 23 negative tests
C Not live. The twelve C programs were compiled once, in the sandbox, with riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc 14.2.0 -O2; the browser receives the machine code, the symbol table and the DWARF line table. There is no compiler in the browser programs/build.sh, programs/build/*.elf

Editing a C program's source has no effect; the source is shown read-only with per-line pipeline marks derived from the DWARF line table. Editing the disassembly of a C program is possible: "Assembly" shows a GNU-style disassembly that reassembles to the identical image (toasm-roundtrip.txt), so a C program can be modified at the instruction level.

Measured, computed, modelled

  • Measured: cycle counts, instruction counts, CPI, stall/flush/forward counts, register and memory contents, pipeline-register values, gate activity. All come from executing the program on the model that is proven identical to the RTL; the Verilator run of every curated program is the reference (programs/build/*.run).
  • Computed: the cell counts and the longest topological path are Yosys outputs over the real netlist. The netlist layout (which gate is drawn where) is Silicon's own grouping by pipeline stage; the placement carries no physical meaning.
  • Not available: physical timing in nanoseconds. There is no timing library for the generic cells; the critical path is reported as logic depth in gate levels (unit delay), see Synthesis.

Layout of the app

  • Pipeline view: the five stages with per-stage contents, the pipeline registers, the three forwarding and bypass lanes (lit when used this cycle), the redirect lane, hazard annotations, register file, memory and the event log.
  • Split: Pipeline + Die view: side-by-side view pairing the 5-stage pipeline datapath with the 8,297-gate Yosys silicon die, register file, and data memory so you can watch instructions flow through IF -> ID -> EX -> MEM -> WB while individual gates toggle 0/1 voltage states in lockstep.
  • Netlist view: the synthesized netlist by stage, zoomable and searchable, with the cells that toggled this cycle or live 0/1 voltage levels highlighted from the gate-level evaluation, a 76-level longest-path overlay, and vector SVG / GDSII die layout exports.
  • Transport bar: reset, step back, step, run/pause, run to end, speed, breakpoints (click an address in the Machine code listing; the run stops when that instruction reaches EX, where it is certain to execute), counters and the cycle timeline.

title: Microarchitecture
html:
Microarchitecture

Silicon implements RV32I (the base integer instruction set, without Zicsr, traps or the M extension) as a classic five-stage in-order pipeline: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB, with four pipeline registers (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB). One instruction can enter and one can leave every cycle; the peak throughput is one instruction per cycle.

 IF          ID               EX                  MEM             WB
 pc ──► imem │ decode, imm    │ fwd mux A/B        │ dmem addr/data │ regfile write
             │ regfile read   │ ALU                │ byte enables   │ (x0 ignored)
             │ (WB bypass)    │ branch/jump target │ load extension │
             │ load-use check │ redirect           │                │
      ◄──────── stall ────────┘                    │                │
      ◄──────── redirect (flush IF/ID, ID/EX) ─────┘                │
                 ▲────────── EX/MEM → EX forwarding ──┘             │
                 ▲────────── MEM/WB → EX forwarding ────────────────┘
                 ▲────────── WB → ID register-file bypass ──────────┘

Interfaces

The core has an instruction port and a data port; the memories live outside the core (in the test bench and in the browser, one 64 KiB RAM serves both ports).

  • Instruction port: imem_addr out, imem_rdata in, combinational (same-cycle) read.
  • Data port: dmem_addr, dmem_wdata, dmem_be[3:0], dmem_we, dmem_re out, dmem_rdata in. Reads are combinational, writes happen at the clock edge. Loads therefore have a one-cycle latency as seen by the pipeline (the data is available in MEM, usable by the next instruction only through forwarding from MEM/WB, hence the load-use stall).
  • halted out, rst is synchronous. Two reset cycles bring every flop to its defined value; fetch starts at PC 0.

Stage by stage

IF. pc is a 32-bit register. The fetched word and its PC go to IF/ID with a valid bit. Prediction is static not-taken: the next PC is always PC + 4 unless EX redirects. If the pipeline is stalled, PC and IF/ID hold their values. After a halt instruction has passed EX, fetch_stopped is set and nothing further is fetched.

ID. The instruction is decoded into an ALU operation, operand selects (PC or rs1; immediate or rs2), the memory operation and the write-back select (ALU, load, PC + 4). The immediate is generated for the I, S, B, U and J formats. The register file (32 × 32 bit, x0 hard-wired to zero) is read combinationally; a write happening in WB in the same cycle is bypassed into the read value (WB → ID bypass), so a producer three instructions ahead needs no forwarding path in EX. Load-use detection also lives here:

stall = idex_valid & idex_mem_read & (idex_rd != 0) & ifid_valid
      & ((id_uses_rs1 & id_rs1 == idex_rd) | (id_uses_rs2 & id_rs2 == idex_rd))

When stall is set the PC and IF/ID hold, and a bubble (valid = 0) is inserted into ID/EX. Exactly one cycle later the load is in MEM and the consumer in EX receives the value through the MEM/WB forwarding path on the following cycle. Operand usage is decoded precisely (id_uses_rs1/id_uses_rs2), so an immediate instruction or a lui after a load does not stall on an accidental register-field match.

EX. Operand A and B each pass through a three-way forwarding mux:

fwd_a = FWD_MEM if exmem_valid & exmem_reg_write & exmem_rd != 0 & exmem_rd == idex_rs1
      else FWD_WB if wb_we & wb_rd == idex_rs1
      else register value read in ID

EX/MEM has priority over MEM/WB because it holds the younger instruction. The value forwarded from EX/MEM is the ALU result, or PC + 4 for jal/jalr; a load in EX/MEM is never forwarded from there (its data does not exist yet), which is exactly the case the load-use stall prevents. The ALU implements add, sub, sll, slt, sltu, xor, srl, sra, or, and; lui passes the immediate through, auipc adds PC and immediate. Branch conditions (beq, bne, blt, bge, bltu, bgeu) are evaluated on the forwarded operands; the target is pc + imm for branches and jal, (rs1 + imm) & ~1 for jalr.

A taken branch or any jump asserts redirect: the PC is loaded with the target and both IF/ID and ID/EX are flushed (two instructions fetched down the wrong path are discarded, so a taken branch costs two cycles). A not-taken branch costs nothing.

MEM. The address is the ALU result. Stores drive dmem_wdata (replicated bytes/halfwords) and byte enables from the low address bits; loads read the word and the extension (lb, lbu, lh, lhu, lw) is done here. Misaligned accesses are not trapped (there are no traps); the arch tests only exercise aligned accesses.

WB. The selected result (ALU, load data or PC + 4) is written to the register file if rd != 0. The written value is also the MEM/WB forwarding source for EX and the bypass source for ID.

Halting

ecall and ebreak are the halt instructions. In EX a halt instruction redirects to its own PC and sets fetch_stopped, so no younger instruction survives; it then drains through MEM and WB and halted is set when it reaches WB. Every older instruction has retired at that point, which makes the final register and memory state well defined. The arch tests end differently: they write to tohost, which the test bench watches.

Illegal instructions, fence and the CSR instructions retire as NOPs (no exception model). fence.i is unnecessary because the instruction port reads the same memory that stores write, with no cache.

Cycle accounting

  • cycle counts clock edges after reset. instret counts instructions reaching WB with valid = 1.
  • A load-use stall adds exactly one cycle; a taken branch or jump adds two (the flushed slots).
  • CPI = cycles ÷ instret, measured on the Verilator run of every program (see Programs and CPI).

Pipeline registers

Register Contents
IF/ID valid, pc, instr
ID/EX valid, pc, instr, rs1/rs2 data, imm, rs1/rs2/rd indices, uses_rs1/uses_rs2, alu_op, operand selects, mem_read/mem_write, funct3, reg_write, wb_sel, branch/jal/jalr/halt
EX/MEM valid, pc, instr, alu result, store data, rd, funct3, mem_read/mem_write, reg_write, wb_sel, halt
MEM/WB valid, pc, instr, alu result, load data, rd, reg_write, wb_sel, halt

The synthesized netlist contains 1,486 flip-flops: these pipeline registers, the PC, the 32 × 31 register-file bits (x0 has none) and the halted/fetch_stopped state.

title: Verification
html:
Verification

Every number below is reproduced by a script in the repository; the raw receipts are in archtest/results.md and test/results/.

Official architecture tests (riscv-arch-test 2.7.4, rv32i_m/I)

The 38 test programs of the RV32I suite were assembled with GNU as 2.45 against Silicon's own target description (archtest/target/: model_test.h uses tohost to end a test; the signature region is dumped by the test bench and compared with the reference signatures shipped in the suite, which were generated from the Sail formal model). Run: make && archtest/run.sh. Each test runs on the RTL under Verilator 5.032.

38 passed, 0 failed. The arithmetic tests run at CPI ≈ 1.00 because they are straight-line code; the branch tests show the two-cycle taken-branch cost. One edit was needed to build the suite: binutils 2.45 rejects the pseudo-instruction la x0, label in jalr-01; it is replaced by two explicit instructions of the same size that also target x0 (no architectural effect, see archtest/run.sh).

Spike was not used as a second reference: Spike reserves addresses 0x0–0xfff for its debug module and the Silicon programs are linked at address 0 (the reset vector). The Sail-generated reference signatures are the authoritative check the suite was designed around.

Targeted hazard and branch tests

test/hazards-rtl.mjs asserts the hazard behaviour directly on the Verilator RTL trace of four assembly programs (32 checks, test/results/hazards-rtl.txt):

Program What is asserted on the RTL trace
hazards.S Cycle 4: add t2,t0,t1 in EX takes t0 from MEM/WB and t1 from EX/MEM, operands 40 and 2, result 42. Cycle 5: sub t3,t2,t1 takes t2 from EX/MEM and t1 from MEM/WB. Cycle 9: lw t5 in EX with addi t6,t5,1 in ID raises stall; cycle 10 holds PC and IF/ID and inserts a bubble; cycle 11 the addi receives the load result from MEM/WB. Cycle 15: beq not taken, no redirect. Cycle 16: bne a3,t6,done taken, redirect to 0x4c; cycle 17 IF/ID and ID/EX are flushed and fetch resumes at 0x4c. Exactly one stall and one branch redirect; halt after 23 cycles, a0 = 103
sum.S Exactly 8 stalls, each with lw t2 in EX and add a0,a0,t2 in ID (the naive loop), none in the scheduled loop; a0 = 1240
branches.S 9 taken branches, each followed by a cycle with IF/ID and ID/EX invalid and PC at the redirect target; a0 = 55
memcopy.S Every store whose data operand is forwarded gets it from MEM/WB (the load result after the load-use stall); 20 stalls

Gate-level simulation vs RTL (Verilator)

test/run-verilator-gate.sh simulates the Yosys output (synth/silicon_gates.v with Yosys's simcells.v) under Verilator and compares it with the RTL simulation on every binary: the per-cycle memory-port trace (imem_addr, dmem_addr, dmem_wdata, dmem_we, dmem_be, dmem_re, halted), the final 64 KiB / 4 MiB memory image and the cycle count must be identical.

Result: 55 of 55 identical (17 curated programs including smoke, 38 arch tests; test/results/verilator-gate.md). The longest run is mandel: 2,288,139 cycles, trace identical line by line.

Browser twin vs RTL

The browser does not run Verilator; it runs core.js, a JavaScript model of the same microarchitecture. test/trace-equivalence.mjs compares its full per-cycle trace line (30 fields: PC, every pipeline register's valid/pc/instr, stall, redirect and target, both forwarding selects, ALU operands and result, write-back port, data-memory port, halted) with the Verilator trace of the RTL:

Suite Result
38 arch tests, every cycle 38/38 identical (archtest-js-vs-rtl.txt)
17 programs: trace prefix (60,000 cycles max per program), final registers, final memory, cycle and instruction counts 17/17 identical (programs-js-vs-rtl.txt)

Browser gate-level evaluator vs RTL

gatesim.js evaluates the real netlist (netlist.compact.json, derived from synth/silicon_netlist.json without loss of cells or connections) in topological order each cycle. test/gate-equivalence.mjs runs it on all 38 arch tests next to the behavioural model and compares the netlist's output ports every cycle: 38/38 identical (archtest-jsgate-vs-rtl.txt). In the app, the gate evaluator is checked against the recorded behavioural trace on every cycle it computes: imem_addr, dmem_addr, dmem_we, dmem_be, dmem_wdata (on writes) and halted (dmem_re is not recorded in the browser's cycle log; the Verilator gate-level run compares it). The "gate-level ≡ RTL · N cycles" chip in the transport bar counts the distinct cycles checked and would turn red on a mismatch.

Session machinery

test/session-gatetrack.mjs (run on hazards, primes, calls, bubble) checks the step-back history, run-to-halt cycle counts against the Verilator run, the final a0, the memory undo log, breakpoint stops, seeking to arbitrary cycles, and the gate tracker's flop state and toggle counts at sampled cycles against a fresh evaluation.

Assembler

See Assembler: 41/41 curated checks byte-identical to GNU as/ld, 110/110 random programs, 23/23 negative tests, and the disassembly-to-source round trip on all programs.

Reproduce

make all gate                 # Verilator RTL and gate-level simulators
archtest/run.sh               # 38 arch tests -> archtest/results.md
programs/build.sh             # compile, run and record all programs
test/run-all.sh               # every JS-side suite -> test/results/*.txt (~40 s)
test/run-verilator-gate.sh    # gate vs RTL on all 55 binaries (~4 min)

title: Synthesis report
html:
Synthesis report

Yosys 0.52 synthesizes rtl/silicon_core.sv to a flat netlist of generic cells. The script (synth/synth.ys):

read_verilog -sv rtl/silicon_core.sv
hierarchy -check -top silicon_core
synth -top silicon_core -flatten
dfflegalize -cell $_DFF_P_ 01 -cell $_DFFE_PP_ 01 -cell $_SDFF_PP?_ 01 -cell $_SDFFE_PP?P_ 01
abc -g AND,NAND,OR,NOR,XOR,XNOR,MUX
opt_clean -purge
tee -o synth/stat.txt stat
tee -o synth/ltp.txt ltp -noff
write_json synth/silicon_netlist.json
write_verilog -noattr -noexpr synth/silicon_gates.v

dfflegalize restricts the sequential cells to positive-edge flops with optional enable and synchronous reset; ABC maps all combinational logic onto two-input gates plus a 2:1 multiplexer. There is no memory macro: the register file is synthesized to flip-flops and multiplexers, which is why MUX and NAND dominate.

Cell counts (synth/stat.txt)

Cell Count Role
$NAND 2298 combinational
$MUX 1784 combinational (register-file read trees, forwarding muxes, write-back select)
$AND 1234 combinational
$DFFE_PP 992 flop with enable: the 31 × 32 register-file bits
$OR 781 combinational
$SDFFE_PP0P 474 flop with synchronous reset and enable: PC, IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB, halted, fetch_stopped (the enable is the stall hold or ~halted)
$NOT 396 combinational
$XOR 119 combinational (adder, comparators)
$XNOR 116 combinational
$NOR 83 combinational
$SDFF_PP0 10 flop with synchronous reset: the two 5-bit register-read address fields of IF/ID (rdaddr1, rdaddr2)
$DFF_P 10 plain flop: the ID/EX ALU-operation code, which Yosys's fsm pass extracted as a state register and re-encoded one-hot (4-bit binary with 11 reachable codes in the RTL; 10 state flops remain after optimization; synth/yosys.log)
Total 8297 6811 combinational cells, 1486 flip-flops

Nets: 8,368 (Yosys bit ids, plus two constants) in the compact form the browser loads; 11 ports. Yosys names a flop after the net it drives, so in the netlist view the PC appears as imem_addr[31:0], the EX/MEM ALU result mostly as dmem_addr[...], and the IF/ID instruction as its decoded fields (id_opcode, id_rd, id_funct3, rdaddr1, rdaddr2, id_funct7, id_imm). The RTL names Yosys merged away are kept as aliases (39 bits, e.g. exmem_alu[31:2] = dmem_addr[31:2], exmem_store_data[7:0] = dmem_wdata[7:0]), so searching for the RTL name finds the same flops and says which name Yosys gave them.

Estimated critical path

There is no timing library for these generic cells, so there is no path delay in nanoseconds; Yosys's ltp (longest topological path, -noff stops at flip-flops) gives the logic depth in gate levels:

  • Longest path: 76 levels, from the flop memwb_rd[4] (the destination-register field in MEM/WB) through the forwarding comparators and operand muxes into the ALU and out to alu_y[31], which is captured by the dmem_addr[31] flop (the EX/MEM ALU-result register; Yosys names flops after the net they drive).
  • This is the expected critical path of a forwarding five-stage pipeline: forwarding-select compare → 3:1 operand mux → 32-bit adder carry chain → result mux. The branch comparison and jump-target adder share most of the depth.
  • The netlist view's "longest path" overlay walks the compact netlist in the browser and highlights one path of the same length (76 levels); several paths tie at that length, so the highlighted flops can differ from the Yosys printout.

What this means: with unit delay per gate the clock period would be about 76 gate delays plus setup and clock-to-Q. A timing-annotated flow (a real cell library plus OpenSTA) was not run; the unit-delay depth is the only timing figure reported, and it is labelled as such in the app.

Gate-level equivalence

The gate-level netlist (synth/silicon_gates.v) was simulated under Verilator against the RTL on all 55 binaries with identical port traces and memory images (see Verification). The browser evaluates the same netlist (netlist.compact.json: identical 8,297 cells and connectivity, with a stage assignment and a 2-D placement for drawing) and checks its ports against the behavioural model on every computed cycle.

Toolchain

Tool Version
Yosys 0.52
Verilator 5.032
Icarus Verilog 12.0 (installed; the receipts use Verilator)
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc 14.2.0
GNU binutils (as, ld, objdump) 2.45
Node.js 20.20.2

title: Programs and CPI
html:
Programs and CPI

Eighteen curated programs: twelve in C (compiled in the sandbox with riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc 14.2.0, flags -g -march=rv32i -mabi=ilp32 -O2 -ffreestanding -fno-builtin -nostdlib -nostartfiles, linked with programs/crt0.S, programs/link.ld and -lgcc into a 64 KiB RAM at address 0) and six in assembly. Each one ends with ebreak and leaves its result in a0. The browser receives the machine code, symbols and line table; the assembly programs can be edited and reassembled in the browser.

Measured CPI

Cycles and instructions are from the Verilator run of the RTL (programs/build/<name>.run); stalls, flushes and forwards are counted on the browser twin, whose per-cycle trace is identical to the RTL's (Verification). The identity cycles = 4 + instructions + stalls + 2 × flushes holds for every program: four cycles of pipeline fill, one cycle per load-use stall, two discarded fetch slots per taken branch or jump.

Program Source Result in a0 Cycles Instructions CPI Load-use stalls Flushes (redirects) EX forwards WB bypasses
primes — Sieve of Eratosthenes C 541 (0x21d) 16,700 11,451 1.4584 279 2,483 2,022 1,260
quicksort — Quicksort (Lomuto) C 760 (0x2f8) 1,021 817 1.2497 0 100 185 199
fibonacci_matrix — Fibonacci 2x2 Matrix Power C 832040 (0xcb228) 2,340 1,624 1.4409 0 356 420 82
fib — Fibonacci table C 832040 (0xcb228) 456 324 1.4074 0 64 66 2
gcd — Binary GCD C 21 (0x15) 864 554 1.5596 0 153 272 42
bubble — Bubble sort C 62 (0x3e) 1,326 842 1.5748 120 180 289 242
crc32 — CRC-32 (bitwise) C 1475291997 (0x57ef2b5d) 2,570 2,032 1.2648 0 267 1,129 265
matmul — 3x3 matrix multiply C 175 (0xaf) 1,075 749 1.4352 0 161 178 39
strrev — String reverse C 25 (0x19) 330 249 1.3253 1 38 7 77
bsearch — Binary search C 21 (0x15) 377 295 1.2780 0 39 85 32
collatz — Collatz chains C 97 (0x61) 24,841 17,975 1.3820 0 3,431 9,649 198
mandel — Mandelbrot (fixed point) C 144 (0x90) 2,288,139 1,605,069 1.4256 144 341,461 522,126 21,901
hazards — Hazards, one at a time asm 103 (0x67) 23 16 1.4375 1 1 13 1
branches — Counting loop asm 55 (0x37) 56 34 1.6471 0 9 21 2
sum — Load-use: naive vs scheduled asm 1240 (0x4d8) 127 87 1.4598 8 14 24 11
multiply — Shift-and-add multiply asm 56088 (0xdb18) 83 53 1.5660 0 13 19 1
memcopy — Byte copy and word copy asm 32 (0x20) 188 128 1.4688 20 18 40 4
calls — Calls and a stack frame asm 74 (0x4a) 98 66 1.4848 0 14 22 17

"Flushes" counts redirects from EX (taken branches, jal, jalr); the final ebreak is not counted because nothing younger needs to retire. "EX forwards" counts operands taken from EX/MEM or MEM/WB in EX; "WB bypasses" counts register-file reads in ID that saw the value being written in WB that same cycle.

Expected outputs

  • primes (Sieve of Eratosthenes): a0 = 541 (the 100th prime); primes[0..99] in memory. Watch: Byte stores (sb) marking composite[] in the inner loop; the final loop collects primes[] with a load-use stall on every candidate.
  • fib (Fibonacci table): a0 = 832040 = fib(30); fib[0..31] in memory. Watch: The running sum is forwarded EX/MEM to EX on every iteration; each sw depends on a value computed one instruction earlier.
  • gcd (Binary GCD): a0 = 21 = gcd(1071, 462); the g field of every table entry is filled in. Watch: Shift loops where each srli feeds the next andi; the loop-exit branches flush two fetched instructions each time.
  • bubble (Bubble sort): a0 = 62 swaps; data[16] sorted ascending in memory. Watch: Compare-and-swap pairs in the memory view; back-to-back lw/lw/bgeu with a load-use stall before the compare.
  • crc32 (CRC-32 (bitwise)): a0 = 0x57ef2b5d, the same value zlib.crc32 computes for the message. Watch: The 8-step inner loop is a dependent chain (andi, neg, and, srli, xor): every ALU result is forwarded to the next instruction.
  • matmul (3x3 matrix multiply): a0 = 175 = trace(C); C[3][3] in memory. Watch: RV32I has no multiply instruction: GCC calls libgcc __mulsi3. Each call and return is a redirect that flushes the front end.
  • strrev (String reverse): a0 = 25 (length); text[] reversed in place. Watch: lbu/sb pairs swap characters from both ends; the ASCII column of the memory view flips while it runs.
  • bsearch (Binary search): a0 = 21 (index of 733); found[4] and probes[4] in memory. Watch: Data-dependent branches: each probe is a lw followed by two compares, one taken and one not, flushing on every taken branch.
  • collatz (Collatz chains): a0 = 97 (longest chain below 100); best_steps = 118; steps[1..99] in memory. Watch: The parity test (andi, bnez) decides between a shift and a slli+add+addi chain; branch outcomes alternate unpredictably.
  • mandel (Mandelbrot (fixed point)): a0 = 144 bounded points; 12 rows of 40 characters at image[]. Watch: Long run (2.29 M cycles): press Run. The ASCII image appears row by row in memory at image[]; most time is spent in __mulsi3.
  • hazards (Hazards, one at a time): a0 = 103. Watch: Step from reset. Cycle 4: add t2,t0,t1 takes t0 from MEM/WB and t1 from EX/MEM. Cycle 9: addi t6,t5,1 waits in ID for one cycle while lw t5 is in EX (load-use stall). Cycle 16: bne is taken and the two instructions fetched after it are flushed.
  • branches (Counting loop): a0 = 55, a1 = 10. Watch: Nine taken branches, each flushing two wrongly fetched instructions (the core predicts not-taken); the last blt falls through.
  • sum (Load-use: naive vs scheduled): a0 = a1 = 1240. Watch: The first loop stalls one cycle per element (lw immediately followed by add). The second loop does the same work with the pointer and counter updates moved between them: no stalls.
  • multiply (Shift-and-add multiply): a0 = 56088 = 123 x 456. Watch: andi t0 -> beqz t0 is a forwarded compare; the loop runs 9 times for a 9-bit multiplier.
  • memcopy (Byte copy and word copy): a0 = 32; dst_bytes and dst_words equal src. Watch: lbu/sb pairs then lw/sw pairs; the store data is forwarded from the load result in WB. Both destination buffers fill in the memory view.
  • calls (Calls and a stack frame): a0 = 74 = 77 + 55. Watch: jal writes ra from PC+4 in WB; ret is a jalr whose target comes from a forwarded ra. sp moves down and back up in the register file.

The final register and memory images of every program are recorded in programs/build/<name>.run and <name>.mem; the app compares a finished run's a0 with the recorded value ("same as the Verilator run"). A seventeenth program, smoke, is used only by the test scripts.

Why the CPI is what it is

  • Straight-line arithmetic (the arch tests) runs at CPI ≈ 1.00.
  • Every taken branch costs two cycles because the core predicts not-taken and resolves in EX. branches (a counting loop) is the worst case at 1.65; collatz and mandel sit around 1.4 because their loop bodies are longer.
  • Load-use stalls cost one cycle; sum shows the same work with and without them (8 stalls in the naive loop, none in the scheduled loop).
  • RV32I has no multiply: matmul and mandel call libgcc's __mulsi3, so most of mandel's 2.29 M cycles are shift-and-add loops inside that routine.

title: Assembler
html:
Assembler

asm.js is a two-pass RV32I assembler written for this app. It accepts the GNU as dialect used by the curated programs and produces the same bytes GNU as + ld produce for them.

Accepted input

  • Labels, including numeric local labels (1:, 1b, 1f); . for the current address.
  • Sections: .text, .data, .rodata, .bss, .section name (recognised by prefix: .text*, .data*/.rodata*/.sdata*/.srodata*, .bss*/.sbss*). Layout follows programs/link.ld: text at 0, then data (4-aligned), then bss.
  • Data: .word/.long/.int, .half/.short/.2byte, .byte, .ascii, .asciz/.string, .space/.skip/.zero, .align/.p2align (power of two), .balign, .equ/.set. .globl, .option, .type, .size, .file, .ident, .attribute are accepted and ignored.
  • Expressions: + - * / % << >> & | ^ ~ ( ), decimal, hex (0x), binary (0b), character literals with escapes, symbols, and the relocation functions %hi, %lo, %pcrel_hi, %pcrel_lo.
  • All 37 RV32I base instructions plus fence, ecall, ebreak, and the standard pseudo-instructions: nop, li (one or two instructions, matching GNU's choice), la, mv, not, neg, seqz, snez, sltz, sgtz, beqz, bnez, blez, bgez, bltz, bgtz, bgt, ble, bgtu, bleu, j, jr, jal offset, jalr rs, ret, call, tail, and the lw rd, symbol / sw rs, symbol, rt forms.
  • Register names: x0–x31 and ABI names (zero, ra, sp, gp, tp, t0–t6, s0/fp–s11, a0–a7).
  • Linker relaxation is reproduced: la and symbol-addressed loads/stores shrink to a single x0-relative instruction when the address fits in 12 bits, as GNU ld does for this memory map, so listings match objdump byte for byte.

Errors

Errors are reported with the source line (for example line 2: unknown instruction 'addx') and nothing is loaded. The negative test suite (test/asm-errors.mjs, 23 cases) covers unknown instructions and directives, wrong operand counts, bad registers, out-of-range immediates, branch and jump offsets that do not fit or are misaligned, undefined and duplicate labels, malformed expressions and strings, bad alignment arguments, and la into zero.

Tests

Test Result
test/asm-vs-gnu.mjs: the 7 curated assembly sources assembled and compared with the GNU-built image byte for byte; the objdump listing of all 17 programs (C included) re-assembled word for word; the browser disassembler's output for every instruction re-assembled to the same word 41/41
test/asm-fuzz-vs-gnu.mjs: random programs (every instruction form, random immediates, labels, data directives, expressions), assembled by both assemblers and compared 110/110 (seeds 1, 7, 3: 40 + 40 + 30 programs)
test/asm-errors.mjs: inputs that must be rejected, with the expected message 23/23
test/toasm-roundtrip.mjs: toasm.js turns each program's machine code into GNU-style source (the Assembly tab of a C program), which reassembles to the identical image all 16 curated programs

The assembler is used live in the browser: "Assemble & load" (Ctrl+Enter) assembles the editor contents, loads the image into a fresh 64 KiB memory, resets the core and keeps the line-to-address map so the pipeline marks in the editor gutter follow the instructions.

title: Limitations
html:
Limitations

Processor

  • RV32I only. No M extension (GCC is invoked with -march=rv32i; multiplications become calls to libgcc's __mulsi3), no Zicsr, no counters readable from software, no privilege modes, no traps or exceptions. Illegal and CSR instructions retire as NOPs; misaligned loads and stores are not detected.
  • ecall and ebreak halt the core; there is no environment to call into.
  • Static not-taken branch prediction, resolved in EX: every taken branch or jump costs two cycles. No branch predictor, no return-address stack.
  • Memory is a flat 64 KiB RAM (4 MiB in the arch-test bench) with combinational reads and no caches; instruction and data ports read the same array, so self-modifying code works without fence.i. The core has no bus interface, interrupts or peripherals.
  • The design is a teaching-scale core and has not been through a physical flow: no timing library, no placement, no clock-tree, no power numbers. The reported critical path is a unit-delay logic depth (76 levels).

Verification

  • Arch tests are run against the reference signatures of riscv-arch-test 2.7.4 (RV32I, 38 tests). Spike was not used as a second oracle: the Silicon programs are linked at address 0, which Spike reserves for its debug module, and relinking them elsewhere would change the programs being verified.
  • The gate-level comparison under Verilator checks the port traces (every memory access, every cycle) and the final memory images, which together determine the architectural outcome; it does not compare the internal flops of the gate netlist with the RTL (their names differ after synthesis). The browser evaluator additionally checks the netlist's port outputs against the behavioural model every cycle.
  • Equivalence between the browser twin and the RTL is established by trace comparison over the arch tests (complete) and the curated programs (complete for programs up to 60,000 cycles; for mandel the first 60,000 cycles plus the final state). It is not a formal proof: a user program can in principle reach a state no test reached. The gate-level evaluator's per-cycle port check in the app is the runtime guard for that case; a mismatch would be shown in the transport bar.
  • Random instruction-stream testing of the core itself was not done; the assembler fuzzer tests the assembler, not the pipeline.

App

  • C is compiled in the sandbox, not in the browser. The C source view is read-only; editing is possible at the instruction level in the Assembly tab (the disassembly reassembles to the identical image).
  • The in-browser assembler covers the GNU as dialect used by the curated programs (see Assembler). It does not support macros, .include, .rept, .irp, multiple files, floating-point or compressed instructions, or relocations to external symbols.
  • Programs are limited to 64 KiB of memory and 3 million cycles per run (mandel, the longest curated program, is 2.29 M cycles; it takes well under a minute at full speed in the browser). Gate-level activity for a cycle far from the last computed one is reconstructed by replaying the netlist from the nearest keyframe (every 256 cycles); a progress bar is shown for long replays.
  • Gate-level activity is computed for the cycle being viewed. During fast runs the netlist view catches up when the run stops; it does not animate every intermediate cycle at thousands of cycles per second.
  • The netlist layout groups cells by pipeline stage and register-file bank; it is a reading aid, not a placement. Wires are drawn only for a cell's immediate neighbours at high zoom.
  • Step back uses a history ring of the last 4,096 cycles; seeking further back replays the program from reset to the requested cycle (a progress bar is shown), so every cycle is reachable but far seeks in long runs take a moment.
  • No persistence: an edited program lives in the page until it is reloaded. Nothing is sent anywhere; the app is static.
